<description>
{
 "summary": "Updates the legacy-to-SQLite wallet migration process to skip copying legacy records and transaction records upfront rather than copying and subsequently erasing them. Because migration generates replacement descriptor records and rewrites all transactions, filtering these record types during MigrateToSQLite avoids redundant database disk writes. With the deletion step removed, the PR deletes several unused database erase helpers (EraseTx, RemoveTxs, DeleteRecordsWithDB, EraseRecords) and makes HasLegacyRecords static to walletdb.cpp.",
 "problem": "Legacy wallet migration dumps all BDB records into a new SQLite database, only for subsequent steps to immediately erase legacy key/script records and delete or overwrite transaction records. This incurs unnecessary disk I/O and keeps dead record-erasure code paths in the wallet.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"The legacy wallet records are replaced with descriptor records produced during migration, and transaction records are already being rewritten by migration, so not writing them in the first place is also fine. This allows us to remove several database record erase functions, specifically EraseTx and EraseRecords.\""

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
